name: Genetic epilepsy with febrile seizures plus (GEFS+)
aliases: generalised epilepsy with febrile seizures plus

reference.source: ILAE classification / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: GEFS+ is a familial epilepsy spectrum rather than a single syndrome, defined by variable phenotypes clustering within a family
The core phenotype is febrile seizures plus, in which febrile seizures continue beyond the usual age of six years or are accompanied by afebrile seizures
The spectrum spans mild febrile seizures at one end to severe phenotypes including Dravet syndrome at the other
Inheritance is typically autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity within a pedigree
Implicated genes include those encoding sodium channel subunits (SCN1A, SCN1B) and GABA-A receptor subunits (GABRG2)
A careful family history is essential and often reveals relatives with differing seizure types
Most milder phenotypes have a good prognosis, but the possibility of a severe end-of-spectrum case warrants vigilance
reference.pathophysiology: GEFS+ is a genetically heterogeneous familial epilepsy in which variants in ion-channel and neurotransmitter-receptor genes, notably sodium channel subunits (SCN1A, SCN1B) and the GABA-A receptor subunit GABRG2, alter neuronal excitability. These variants shift the balance between excitation and inhibition, lowering the seizure threshold particularly during fever. Incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity, influenced by modifier genes and the specific variant, explain why the same familial variant can produce anything from isolated febrile seizures to a severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy such as Dravet syndrome.
additionalDifferentials: Dravet syndrome (severe end of the spectrum)
Childhood absence and other genetic generalised epilepsies
additionalInvestigations: Detailed three-generation family history of seizures
Gene panel testing including SCN1A, SCN1B and GABRG2 where indicated
EEG to characterise afebrile seizure types
Brain MRI when focal features or atypical course raise concern for a structural cause
Developmental assessment to identify severe-spectrum cases early
redFlags: Prolonged or frequent seizures suggesting evolution toward a severe phenotype
Developmental slowing raising concern for Dravet syndrome within the spectrum
Onset of afebrile generalised or focal seizures beyond expected febrile-seizure age
Cluster of severe phenotypes within the family pedigree
reference.prognosis: Most individuals, particularly those with febrile seizures or febrile seizures plus, have a good prognosis with seizures that remit in childhood or adolescence and normal development. A minority at the severe end of the spectrum have drug-resistant epilepsy and developmental impairment.
pitfalls: Regarding GEFS+ as a single benign entity and overlooking severe-spectrum cases
Failing to take a detailed family history that reveals the diagnosis
Assuming persistence of febrile seizures beyond six years is always benign
Not reconsidering the diagnosis when development slows or seizures become refractory
management: Antiseizure medication for ongoing afebrile seizures, favouring broad-spectrum agents such as sodium valproate or levetiracetam
Avoid sodium-channel-blocking drugs such as carbamazepine and lamotrigine where an SCN1A/Dravet-spectrum phenotype is suspected, as they can aggravate seizures
Fever management with antipyretics and a home rescue benzodiazepine protocol for prolonged or clustering seizures
For severe Dravet-spectrum disease, adjunctive agents such as stiripentol, cannabidiol or fenfluramine
Developmental surveillance to identify severe-spectrum cases early and provide educational and rehabilitative support
Genetic counselling for the autosomal dominant inheritance with incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity, informed by a three-generation family history
Refer to neurology or a specialist epileptology and clinical genetics service for phenotyping and long-term management
